items.stem: An inflation target of 2% ± 1% means the central bank aims for inflation
options: between 1% and 3%, with 2% as the central target
items.answer: between 1% and 3%, with 2% as the central target
items.markingKey: Symmetric target band.

items.stem: Explain why a persistent current account deficit may be a problem.
items.answer: It must be financed by borrowing or asset sales abroad, increasing foreign debt and interest payments; it may lead to a sharp depreciation or loss of confidence; it can indicate a lack of competitiveness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: financing/debt; 1 mark: risk of currency crisis/competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Explain why a more equal distribution of income may be a macroeconomic objective.
items.answer: Reduces poverty and social tension, may raise aggregate demand (poor have higher MPC), improves health and human capital, supports sustainable growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Pelora has GDP of $400 billion and a current account balance of $30 billion. Calculate the current account balance as a percentage of GDP.

Istrana has GDP of $1200 billion, a current account balance of $30 billion and inflation of 2.4%. The inflation target is 2% ± 1%. Calculate the current account as a % of GDP and assess the economy’s performance against its inflation and external balance objectives.
items.answer: CA = 2.5% of GDP. Inflation is within the target band. A small imbalance is likely sustainable.
items.markingKey: 30/1200 × 100 [1]; compare inflation with 1–3% [1]; judgement on external balance [2].

items.stem: Extract: Latest data for Nordavia: unemployment 3.5%, inflation 6.2% (target 2% ± 1%), current account -5.1% of GDP, real GDP growth 4.0%. The natural rate of unemployment is estimated at 5%. (a) Using a Phillips curve diagram, explain the relationship between the unemployment and inflation data. (b) Explain one limitation of the data in judging macroeconomic performance.
items.answer: (a) Unemployment below natural rate with high inflation: movement up SRPC; expectations may shift it. (b) Revisions, hidden unemployment, CPI biases, informal sector, distribution not shown.

items.stem: Inflation in Esteria has fallen below zero for the first time in decades. Explain why the central bank may be concerned.
items.answer: Deflation raises the real value of debt, may lead consumers to delay purchases, depressing AD; nominal interest rates cannot fall far below zero, limiting policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each concern [2]

items.stem: Westaria has GDP of $1200 billion and a current account balance of −$16 billion. Calculate the current account balance as a percentage of GDP.
Zentara has GDP of $500 billion and a current account balance of −$16 billion. Calculate the current account balance as a percentage of GDP.

Marvona has GDP of $500 billion, a current account balance of −$30 billion and inflation of 3.8%. The inflation target is 2% ± 1%. Calculate the current account as a % of GDP and assess the economy’s performance against its inflation and external balance objectives.
items.answer: CA = -6% of GDP. Inflation is outside the target band. A deficit above 3–4% of GDP may be unsustainable.
items.markingKey: -30/500 × 100 [1]; compare inflation with 1–3% [1]; judgement on external balance [2].

items.stem: The short-run Phillips curve shows
options: that inflation and unemployment are unrelated
a positive relationship between unemployment and inflation
an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
the link between growth and unemployment
items.answer: an inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation
items.markingKey: Lower unemployment associated with higher wage/price inflation.

items.stem: With the aid of a diagram, explain why there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.
items.answer: Diagram: inflation vertical, unemployment horizontal; LRPC vertical at natural rate Un; SRPC1 for expected inflation 2%. Expansionary policy moves along SRPC1 to lower unemployment and higher inflation (4%). Workers revise expectations to 4%, SRPC shifts up to SRPC2 and unemployment returns to Un with inflation at 4%.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: LRPC; 1 mark: movement along SRPC; 1 mark: expectations shift SRPC; 1 mark: return to Un at higher inflation [4]

items.stem: Explain how a supply shock such as a rise in oil prices affects the Phillips curve.
items.answer: Costs rise, causing higher inflation and lower output/employment at the same time: the SRPC shifts up/right (stagflation).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cost-push; 1 mark: SRPC shifts outward [2]

items.stem: In Korvia, the expectations-augmented Phillips curve is π = πᵉ − 2(u − 4), where π is inflation, πᵉ expected inflation and u the unemployment rate (%). Expected inflation is 3%. Calculate inflation if unemployment is 3%.

In Loristan, the expectations-augmented Phillips curve is π = πᵉ − 0.5(u − 6), where π is inflation, πᵉ expected inflation and u the unemployment rate (%). Expected inflation is 4% and the government holds unemployment at 4%. (a) Calculate inflation this year. (b) If expectations next year equal this year’s inflation, calculate next year’s inflation. (c) Explain what this implies about holding unemployment below its natural rate.
items.answer: (a) 5% (b) 6% (c) Inflation accelerates each year: unemployment can only be held below the natural rate (6%) at the cost of ever-rising inflation; in the long run the Phillips curve is vertical.
items.markingKey: (a) substitution [1]; (b) πᵉ = 5% → π = 6% [2]; (c) accelerating inflation / vertical LRPC / natural rate = NAIRU [2].

items.stem: In Rovania, the expectations-augmented Phillips curve is π = πᵉ − 0.5(u − 4), where π is inflation, πᵉ expected inflation and u the unemployment rate (%). (c) Explain what this implies about holding unemployment below its natural rate.

items.answer: adjusting nominal GDP growth for inflation

items.stem: Explain two limitations of using a consumer price index to measure inflation.
items.answer: The basket and weights may not reflect all households; quality changes and new products are hard to include; substitution bias; excludes some housing costs.
